So, I’ve finalised a generic pattern for business RDNH overcharge: 

{noformat}SELECT 
	oc.country,
	date_trunc('month',oc.calculation_date) AS calc_month, 
	approx_distinct(oc.order_token_id,0.0041) AS count_orders,
	round(sum(oc.actual_price_eur)) AS sum_charges_eur
	FROM ng_public.etl_driver_overcharge_check oc
	WHERE oc.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -3, current_date) as date)
	AND oc.payment_method = 'business'
	AND oc.country = 'gh'
	AND oc.decision = 'pass'
--	AND oc.order_token_id IN (1773636433,1733556519,1766247581,1770697626,1773358736)
	AND oc.actual_duration_in_min*1.000/oc.predicted_duration_in_min < 0.6
	AND oc.actual_distance_in_meters*1.000/oc.predicted_distance_in_meters < 0.2
	AND (oc.actual_distance_in_meters + oc.arrived_to_driving_distance) *1.000/oc.predicted_distance_in_meters < 0.5 -- fallback if driver forgets to start trip
	GROUP BY 1,2
	ORDER BY 2 ASC{noformat}

!Screenshot 2025-07-11 at 15.34.17.png|width=100%,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-11 at 15.34.17.png"!

Will expectedly touch around *6-7K eur* in a month from around 200-350 orders.

The pattern fits almost identically another business scenario in NL: [https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fraud/rules/edit/driver_overcharge_check/OVERCHARGE_TO_ZERO_LOCAL_PATTERN|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fraud/rules/edit/driver_overcharge_check/OVERCHARGE_TO_ZERO_LOCAL_PATTERN] we can reuse this rule to add this pattern.

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

{noformat} , driver_car_activity AS (
    SELECT

        , country.country_code
        , SUM(car_driver.sum_driver_waiting_orders_time_seconds_local) / 60 AS waiting_minutes
        , SUM(car_driver.sum_driver_order_time_seconds_local) / 60 AS order_minutes
        , SUM(car_driver.rides_order_tries_in_finished_state_local) AS finished_rides
        , SUM(car_driver.rides_price_before_discounts_local) AS gmv
        , SUM(car_driver.rides_price_before_discounts_eur_local) AS gmv_eur
    FROM mart_models_spark.mart_car_driver_city_hour_local car_driver
        LEFT JOIN core_models_spark.dim_country country ON car_driver.order_country_id = country.country_id
    WHERE
        calendar_date_local >= DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC('week',CAST('{0}' as TIMESTAMP)), 28)
        AND calendar_date_local < DATE_TRUNC('week',CAST('{0}' as TIMESTAMP))
        AND order_city_id IN (SELECT id from city_ids)
        AND ( COALESCE(sum_driver_waiting_orders_time_seconds_local,0) + COALESCE(sum_driver_order_time_seconds_local, 0) ) > 0
    GROUP BY 1,2,3
    )   {noformat}

Hi [~accountid:712020:d008dcec-6cfe-47e4-83a0-c29522744742], hope you are doing great ! 

Thank you very much for your thorough feedback and detailed guidance on the three proposed initiatives. Below you will find our clarifications and additional context for each initiative, along with confirmation of the risks you highlighted and our willingness to adjust the execution accordingly.

h3. 1. “10K Event” – Surprise €5,000 Prize

* We have already launched communications for the 10K Event via email and push notification, clearly stating that a €5,000 prize will be awarded to one randomly selected driver who receives the 10,000th branded sticker.
* The rationale behind the amount is symbolic: we are celebrating the milestone of reaching 10,000 branded cars in France, and this one-time prize reflects the significance of that achievement.
* La Maison du Chauffeur VTC (LMDCVTC) is supporting us in tracking and verifying the 10,000th vehicle.
* All drivers who receive the sticker between the communicated campaign dates are automatically eligible for the prize.
* We have included an asterisk disclaimer in each communication, outlining the dates of the campaign and some brief eligibility details. However, no formal “règlement du jeu” has been written or published, and we acknowledge the legal risks associated with that.
* Regarding fleet-linked drivers: if a winning driver is attached to a fleet, the €5,000 will be transferred to the fleet manager’s account, in line with the standard flow for branding payouts. The fleet manager will be expected to transfer the amount to the driver, as is already the case for fixed incentive payments.
* We’ve noted the taxation concerns.

h3. 2. Branded Cars – Goodie Bag Campaign

* This is strictly positioned as a short-term promotional offer with no entry, no contest mechanism, and no financial value requested from drivers.
* The goodie bag consists of: one low-cost dashcam, one phone charger, and a small chocolate bar—none of which are branded or conditioned to continued service.
* It is clearly marketed as a limited-time promo, offered to all drivers who receive a sticker during the defined period, and not as a reward based on performance or engagement.

h3. 3. €5,000 Promotional Giveaway (aka “Lottery”)

* Every driver who receives a sticker during the communicated campaign period is automatically eligible for this promotional giveaway.
* The €5,000 prize pool will be divided among 10 winners (€500 each). Each winner will receive the funds directly in their Bolt wallet, and the amount will be immediately accessible and withdrawable.
* We understand and accept the recommendation that T&Cs must be drafted and published.

We would be happy to *set up a quick call* to review safer alternatives together and ensure that our incentives remain compliant while achieving our lead generation goals.

Lastly, for your visibility, *all campaigns will end on July 31, 2025*, so we are working with a tight operational window and would appreciate any fast-track guidance or templates you may already have in place.

Thanks again for your support,

Matteo

* Referral program does not materially impact overall lead volume, but may be impactful at the activation level (which incrementality’s is currently not measured ). In UA and KE, attributed referral leads are ~2x more likely to convert from Step 2 Leads to Activations (30-day Window). Interestingly, this is not true for Accra, GH as the activation rate for referral leads is pretty much the same as non-referrals - given the prevalence of fraud in the market, it may be indeed the case that driver referral is really not incremental in this market.
* Unaccounted third variable that could neutralise the effect (e.g. in the case of Accra where model is detecting an uplift rather than the expected drop from the blackout test in the city). Note that acquisition ad spend was stable throughout the measurement period.

Note that while we were not able to detect incrementality in the three pilot markets, such results are not uncommon; similar geo experiment design in online ads yield ~40% of success (i.e. incrementality detected at >90% confidence). We expect improved sensitivity in our measurements as we further refine the methodology. 

*Next Steps (Q3)*

* Retry measurements in UA and KE using cohorted activations i.e. activation dated to signup date as the test metric (NB these are not new experiments).
* Research on city-level experiment design repeat UA experiment with such design (if feasible)

*To Consider in Backlog*

* Repeat experiment in KE as a blackout test instead
* Plan for next round of incrementality experiments, ideally at the city-level. Possible candidates for other markets: PY, RO, FR

Hi [~accountid:712020:13033e65-435c-4794-a380-e007eba7615a] it comes from the Money Laundering Control Act (MLCA) and the Regulations Governing Anti-Money Laundering of Financial Institutions issued by the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC). In Taiwan, Bolt is registered as a Third Party Payment Provider, and as such is required to implement AML/CFT controls, including sanctions screening. Specifically, Article 8(7) of Taiwan’s AML Regulations (issued by the FSC) requires us, as a regulated TPPE, to screen customers and counterparties against the designated sanctions list and take appropriate control measures if a match is found.

This obligation is implemented internally through Section 16 of the Bolt AML Policy, which sets out the procedures for sanctions screening — including the frequency, scope (customers, beneficial owners, and counterparties), and the actions to be taken in case of a positive match.

h2. 🔍 Where Things Stand Now

* The EU Commission [announced|https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20250623IPR29094/green-claims-directive-ep-co-rapporteurs-hold-a-press-conference-at-15-15] plans to *withdraw the Green Claims Directive*
* The proposal *has not been formally withdrawn*, but the Council cancelled the final negotiation meeting (called a trilogue) in [June|https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20250623IPR29094/green-claims-directive-ep-co-rapporteurs-hold-a-press-conference-at-15-15].
* *No new meetings have been scheduled* yet.
* The *Danish Presidency* of the Council (since 1 July) will now lead on what happens next.
* We may hear more *after the EU summer break*, likely in *September*.



h2. 🧾 What Should Businesses Do?

Even if this directive disappears:

* [*Greenwashing enforcement is still happening*|https://www.hoganlovells.com/en/publications/on-hold-eu-pulls-the-plug-on-green-claims-directive] in EU countries under existing laws like the *Unfair Commercial Practices Directive*.
* The [*Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive*|https://energy.ec.europa.eu/news/new-eu-rules-empower-consumers-green-transition-enter-force-2024-03-27_en] (a different directive) will go into effect *from September 2026*, banning vague or unverifiable green claims.

*Bottom line*: the pressure to make green claims accurate and evidence-based *isn’t going away*.

Prepare in invoke task script with required parameters to run on cluster, based on [this|https://github.com/kubedb/redis-docker/blob/release-4.0.11/cluster.sh].

{noformat}#!/bin/bash

set -e

# needs args in following manner:
#    src_node_ip
#    src_node_id
#    dst_node_ip
#    dst_node_id
#    slot_start
#    slot_end
reshard() {
    for i in $(seq $5 $6); do
        redis-cli -c -h $3 cluster setslot ${i} importing $2
        redis-cli -c -h $1 cluster setslot ${i} migrating $4
        while true; do
            key=$(redis-cli -c -h $1 cluster getkeysinslot ${i} 1)
            if [ "" = "$key" ]; then
                echo "there are no key in this slot ${i}"
                break
            fi
            redis-cli -h $1 migrate $3 6379 ${key} 0 5000

According to this PR [https://github.com/redis/redis-doc/pull/1803/files|https://github.com/redis/redis-doc/pull/1803/files|smart-link] , order of setslot should be reversed:

h2. Redis Cluster live resharding explained

The {{CLUSTER SETSLOT}} command is an important piece used by Redis Cluster in order to migrate all the keys contained in one hash slot from one node to another. This is how the migration is orchestrated, with the help of other commands as well. We'll call the node that has the current ownership of the hash slot the {{source}} node, and the node where we want to migrate the {{destination}} node.

# Set the destination node slot to _importing_ state using {{CLUSTER SETSLOT <slot> IMPORTING <source-node-id>}}.
# Set the source node slot to _migrating_ state using {{CLUSTER SETSLOT <slot> MIGRATING <destination-node-id>}}.
# Get keys from the source node with {{CLUSTER GETKEYSINSLOT}} command and move them into the destination node using the {{MIGRATE}} command.
# Send {{CLUSTER SETSLOT <slot> NODE <destination-node-id>}} to the destination node.
# Send {{CLUSTER SETSLOT <slot> NODE <destination-node-id>}} to the source node.
# Send {{CLUSTER SETSLOT <slot> NODE <destination-node-id>}} to the other master nodes (optional).

 Notes:

* The order of step 1 and 2 is important. We want the destination node to be ready to accept {{ASK}} redirections when the source node is configured to redirect.
* The order of step 4 and 5 is important.
The destination node is responsible for propagating the change to the rest of the cluster.
If the source node is informed before the destination node and the destination node crashes before it is set as new slot owner, the slot is left with no owner, even after a successful failover.
* Step 6, sending {{SETSLOT}} to the nodes not involved in the resharding, is not technically necessary since the configuration will eventually propagate itself.
However, it is a good idea to do so in order to stop nodes from pointing to the wrong node for the hash slot moved as soon as possible, resulting in less redirections to find the right node.

I have faced like this problem while working with redis-clustering support for our own project. I found a problem with the redis-trib reshard command. It works fine if no key is stored in slots those are migrating from one master to another.

But redis-5 (still developing, not stable yet) has it's own `redis-cli' that has no problem with resharding command I think. Only for lower versions of 5 it happens.
If you look at the official docs for redis say redis reconfiguration and redis cluster resharding, you'll find what they do internally to reshard.

So I solved the problem by doing those tasks by running a bash script instead of running redis-trib reshard command.

Suppose you want to reshard some slots from a master node to other master node. We'll call the node that has the current ownership of the hash slot the source node, and the node where we want to migrate the destination node.

For each slot do the following steps:

Remember that the order of these steps is important here according to redis official docs.
Send CLUSTER SETSLOT <slot> IMPORTING <source-node-id> to destination node to set the slot to importing state.
Send CLUSTER SETSLOT <slot> MIGRATING <destination-node-id> to source node to set the slot to migrating state.
Get keys from the source node with CLUSTER GETKEYSINSLOT command and move them into the destination node using the following MIGRATE command.

MIGRATE target_host target_port key target_database_id timeout

In Redis Cluster there is no need to specify a database other than 0, but MIGRATE is a general command that can be used for other tasks not involving Redis Cluster.
When the migration process is finally finished, use CLUSTER SETSLOT <slot> NODE <destination-node-id> in both source node and destination node in order to set the slot to their normal state again. The same command is usually sent to all other nodes to avoid waiting for the natural propagation of the new configuration across the cluster.
A simple example bash script to do this is also given here:

source-ip: 172.17.0.5. source-id: 1f70a5107e0042a7d33a9efaf88dbdfecd78076a

destination-ip: 172.17.0.4. destination-id: 7e428bae84697a3882ecad19bd0d13ac7ee97d02

another master ip: 172.17.0.7

for i in `seq 0 5460`; do
    redis-cli -c -h 172.17.0.4 cluster setslot ${i} importing 1f70a5107e0042a7d33a9efaf88dbdfecd78076a
    redis-cli -c -h 172.17.0.5 cluster setslot ${i} migrating 7e428bae84697a3882ecad19bd0d13ac7ee97d02
    while true; do
        key=`redis-cli -c -h 172.17.0.5 cluster getkeysinslot ${i} 1`
        if [ "" = "$key" ]; then
            echo "there are no key in this slot ${i}"
            break
        fi
        redis-cli -h 172.17.0.5 migrate 172.17.0.4 6379 ${key} 0 5000
    done
    redis-cli -c -h 172.17.0.5 cluster setslot ${i} node 7e428bae84697a3882ecad19bd0d13ac7ee97d02
    redis-cli -c -h 172.17.0.4 cluster setslot ${i} node 7e428bae84697a3882ecad19bd0d13ac7ee97d02
    redis-cli -c -h 172.17.0.7 cluster setslot ${i} node 7e428bae84697a3882ecad19bd0d13ac7ee97d02
done
```{noformat}

* Reducing the discount from 50% → 30% drives 5–13% bonus savings across all markets, with mixed GMV outcomes
* Retention effects are not significant, except ZA, although AZ and KE show strong signs of long term re-engagement
* By country:
** ZA & KE stand out for high cost-efficiency with significant bonus savings with post-campaign GMV recovery
** GH & HR have more GMV loss than savings but have strong U/C, suggesting savings can be reinvested effectively
** AZ is efficient with moderate GMV loss
** NG has increased order volume but drives more low value rides (gmv per ride) while not significant yet, trends are directionally positive

*_Decision:_* As duplicate user GMV impacts <1% of total signup GMV and proves minimal or positive long-term impact, we recommend rolling out the lower discount in markets where duplicate share ≥ 5%.
*_Next steps:_* We will be rolling out the lower discount for duplicate users in the 6 tested markets, as well as in 8 additional markets where a higher flat discount is currently offered. In markets with high duplicate share such as the Baltics, no changes will be made, as a lower discount is already in place.

{noformat}WITH RankedRows AS (
    SELECT
        ifcdr.id,
        ifcdr.fee_calculator_id,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ifcdr.fee_calculator_id ORDER BY ifcdr.id) AS row_num
    FROM ng_public.invoicing_fee_calculator_driver_row ifcdr
    WHERE ifcdr.fee_calculator_id IN (
        SELECT ifc.id
        FROM ng_public.invoicing_fee_calculator ifc
                 JOIN ng_public.invoicing_fee_calculator_driver_row ifcdr ON ifc.id = ifcdr.fee_calculator_id
        WHERE ifc.is_active = TRUE
          AND ifc.end_date IS NULL
          AND ifc.created_date > DATE('2025-01-01')
    AND ifcdr.className = 'DriverAppOrderPercentageFeeCalculatorRow'
    AND ifcdr.is_deleted = FALSE
GROUP BY ifc.id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
    )
   AND ifcdr.className = 'DriverAppOrderPercentageFeeCalculatorRow'
   AND ifcdr.is_deleted = FALSE
    )
SELECT id, fee_calculator_id
FROM RankedRows
WHERE row_num = 1;{noformat}

*Malaysia.*  :done: 



Section 129 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2010 [Act 709] (“*PDPA*”) (as amended by the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024) provides the grounds in which the data controller may transfer any personal data to a place outside Malaysia. 

Pursuant to Section 48(g) of the PDPA, the Personal Data Protection Commissioner (“*Commissioner*”) had, on 29 April 2025, issued the Cross Border Personal Data Transfer (CBPDT) Guideline (“*CBPDT Guideline*”): 

# to clarify the requirements to be complied with for each of the grounds specified under Section 129 of the PDPA; and 

# to assist the data controller in determining the applicable grounds that can be relied upon by the data controller for the cross border personal data transfer. 

A data controller may transfer personal data outside Malaysia if one of the following conditions is met:
#* *Substantially Similar Law*: The destination country has in force a law that is substantially similar to the PDPA. Data controllers may conduct a Transfer Impact Assessment (“*TIA*”) to satisfy this condition. 
#* *Adequate Level of Protection*: The destination country provides an adequate level of protection equivalent to the PDPA. Data Controllers may conduct a TIA to satisfy this condition.
#* *Data Subject Consent*: The data subject has given explicit consent to the transfer, after being provided with a personal data protection notice detailing the class of third parties and the purpose of the transfer. Consent must be recorded and maintained.
#* *Contractual Necessity*: The transfer is necessary for the performance of a contract between the data subject and the data controller, or for the conclusion or performance of a contract between the data controller and a third party at the request or in the interests of the data subject. The transfer must be for the fulfilment of a specified purpose and there must be no feasible alternative means to fulfil this specified purpose.
#* *Legal Proceedings*: The transfer is required for legal proceedings, obtaining legal advice, or establishing, exercising, or defending legal rights.
#* *Reasonable Grounds*: The data controller has reasonable grounds to believe the transfer is necessary to avoid or mitigate adverse action against the data subject, it is not practicable to obtain consent for the transfer, and the data subject would have given consent if practicable.
#* *Reasonable Precautions and Due Diligence*: The data controller has taken all reasonable precautions and exercised due diligence to ensure the personal data will not be processed in a manner contrary to the PDPA. Mechanisms that can demonstrate that reasonable precautions and due diligence has been undertaken may include Binding Corporate Rules (“*BCRs*”), Contractual Clauses (_which include the ASEAN Model Contractual Clauses for Cross Border Data Flows and/or EU GDPR Standard Contractual Clauses for the Transfer of Personal Data to Third Countries_), or recognised certifications under an approved certification scheme (_such as Europrivacy, the APEC Cross Border Privacy Rules System Certification or APEC Privacy Recognition for Processors Certification_).



Re DPA Authorisation, there is no formal approval/licensing mechanism from the Malaysian DPA; instead, companies must self‑certify compliance (e.g. perform Transfer Impact Assessments, maintain records, apply Section 129 grounds)

*Solution*
To overcome this data issue on our side, we're proceeding with a pilot for carbon data upload, starting with a subset of locations to manage data quality and reduce manual correcting of data before scaling up to include all locations.

*Issue number 2*

Clearsulting have had our emission methodology for months but only presented to me last Wednesday that for nearly all emissions categories we would have to use custom approaches *off* the Carbon programme i.e. still spreadsheets like we have been using to date. This would mean hardly any of the planned savings of time and increased efficiency.

*Key decision needed from us:*

* Decide if we go with _emissions factors built into the Carbon platform_ or stick with _custom ones_ (e.g. those used by South Pole for our emissions accounting for the past four years). # *Unilateral changes*

Let's begin with the solution offered by Edik: we retain the right to unilaterally change the General Terms. Whatever requires negotiation and mutual approval should be reflected in the Special Terms.

Only if this is a no-go for them, we offer a solution: Bolt has the right to update the T&C unilaterally, but Rimi may notify Bolt within x days that it does not agree with the changes, in which case the terms of the previous contract would remain in force.

# *Responsibility for Goods*

_"I believe Rimi is mistaken in thinking they don’t have agreements with couriers — such agreements do exist"_ -> What agreements does Rimi have with countries? In my understanding, there are no. A courier has an agreement with 1) clients (eaters) who order the food for the delivery services and 2) with Bolt for the platform services. I agree that the business needs to explain the model clearly to Rimi. Additionally, legal can review the T&Cs for Delivery Partners in LV and refer to clauses that set certain delivery standards.

Yes, I agree that the business should explain what Bolt is doing.  Local Ops ([~accountid:5fc110f331795a006f947e12] for LV, [~accountid:60528922695c3900706cc77c] or EE, [~accountid:615d90da9cdb93007288f515] for LT) responsible for couriers shall outline the measures in place to ensure standards similar to Rimi's are met. For example, in LV (and likely the same in LT/EE), we have:

* Hygiene and food safety guidelines co-developed with food authorities, made available to couriers.

* Cleaning supplies and designated areas for bag cleaning at all Bolt Market stores.
* Courier training provided in response to complaints (e.g., on how to transport beverages properly).
* Repeated complaints from clients or partners lead to courier suspension or exclusion.

I agree to this idea, too: adding a clause to the agreement that says something like: “Bolt is not responsible for the goods, but will make reasonable efforts to help resolve any issues related to deliveries in a friendly manner.” 

# *Customer Issue Resolution and Deductions*

I agree with your proposal.

# *Alcohol Sales and Legal Compliance*

Correct, we will not undertake responsibility for alcohol sales compliance. Under the law, responsibility for alcohol sales compliance is mostly with the seller (retailer). However, when it comes to ID checks, the responsibility is also on the courier to check the ID. See memo [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Ojjhfkyl1u2MbseS0aR1XbTSWMHxZxrwMTgRYN1y6DM/edit?tab=t.0], see overview [here|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1gI-GsiCkIqV9vvyEPbRk0BhRXXfCSa8HqmTkPdRi5Lc/edit?gid=0#gid=0] (column F for IDs).

# *Sustainability and Contractual Obligations*

Agree with your stand.

h2. 🇹🇿 *LATRA Data Sharing – Summary Overview*

h3. *What’s Happening*

* *LATRA* (Land Transport Regulatory Authority) in *Tanzania* has requested a list of *~4,000 vehicle license plates* from Bolt.
* The purpose: to *cross-check* these with their own database and ensure that *drivers operating on Bolt hold the required private hire license*.

----

h3. *Key Privacy Concern*

* *At first glance*, license plates appear *non-personal*.
* However, LATRA *already links plates to individual drivers* via:
** Vehicle registration documents
** National ID cards
* This means that *providing the plates effectively identifies individuals*, making this a *personal data disclosure* under privacy law.

----

h3. *Existing Integration with LATRA*

* Bolt already has a *full data integration* with LATRA, including:
** *Trip data*, *vehicle info*, and *driver details* via API
** *Quarterly manual submissions* of updated driver/vehicle databases
** This setup applies to *all operators* in Tanzania and is *seen as mandatory* under local regulatory expectations

** UserUpsellBenefitsCache: {EE@EE:{upsellBenefits:[{benefit:{..},bundle_id:EE}]}, EE@LV:{upsellBenefits:[]}, EE@NULL:{upsellBenefits:[]}, NULL@EE:{upsellBenefits:[]}, NULL@LV:{upsellBenefits:[]}, NULL@NULL:{upsellBenefits:[]}}
* If we changed offer’s availability to GLOBAL, only OfferLookupCache and OfferCache would be invalidated right away
** OfferLookupCache: APPROVED_GLOBAL_OFFERS: {offerIds:[EE]}
** OfferCache: {EE:{availability:GLOBAL}}
* OfferEnrollmentCache’s SQL filters out enrollments into GLOBAL offers, so it could contain stale data for EE@* users for up to 12h. However, OfferEnrollmentCache is only accessed via UserOfferService, which will include the EE offer ID from OfferLookupCache (up to date) and offer data from OfferCache (up to date)
* For data returned from UserOfferService:
** EE@EE would continue seeing EE offer
** EE@LV would continue seeing nothing
** *EE@NULL saw EE offer before but would not see it immediately after change*
** *NULL@EE didn’t see EE offer before but would see it after*
** NULL@LV didn’t see EE offer before and wouldn’t see after
** NULL@NULL didn’t see EE offer before and wouldn’t see after change
* MenuNotificationCache depends on UserOfferService and uses the enrollment creation timestamp (for enrolled offers) from OfferEnrollmentCache, but only when offer’s availability is ENROLLMENT. Due to up-to-date OfferCache we would filter out enrollment-based notifications, so the result is correct immediately. Global offers use offer start timestamp for determining if notification is active, but EE offer will be considered too old for notifications after rollout. MenuNotificationCache expiration is 5m, so during that time:
** *EE@EE would be affected (could see notification before, shouldn’t see now, up to 5min)*
** Others would not be affected (couldn’t see before, shouldn’t see now)
* UserUpsellBenefitsCache (30min expiration), UpsellOfferCache (10min expiration) depend on UserOfferService, so:
** *EE@NULL and NULL@EE would be affected (offers list changes, up to 30min)*
** Others would not be affected (no offer list change)

In conclusion:

* EE@EE could possibly see menu notification when there’s none for up to 5min
* EE@NULL would not see EE offer in offers list anymore (but would have direct access to it)
* NULL@EE would start seeing EE offer in offers list, but would not see upsell in eater app for up to 30min
* Others would not be affected

{quote}Dear Rafael,



Thank you for your questions relating to selfie verification. Please note the following:



* Bolt drivers are required to undergo a selfie verification check when they first register as a driver, and thereafter must undergo additional selfie checks either: (a) periodically; or (b) when certain events are triggered on their account. Completing selfie verification is mandatory in order to go online and take trips.
* The purpose of selfie checks is to ensure that the relevant person matches who they are representing to be (in particular, to verify that the person using the driver account is the same as the person who submitted the driver’s licence on the account). This limits the scope of fraudulent or harmful activity by preventing driver impersonation and account sharing.
* The use of facial recognition technology during the selfie verification process is optional, and drivers can instead choose for their selfie to be verified manually by a member of Bolt’s team. Our specialist team are currently investigating your account to ensure that when you are next asked to complete the verification process, you should be presented with the option to have your selfie manually reviewed. Please note that our specialist team require an additional week to complete their review in this regard, as they have experienced technical difficulties in retrieving relevant information. We apologise for any inconvenience caused by this extension. Please let us know if you experience any issues in this regard.
* To be clear, Bolt is not selling the data you have provided as part of the selfie verification process.

I believe that The current Swiss driver T&Cs provide a *sufficient basis* to implement the suggested process, provided it is applied in a transparent and proportionate manner. 


Specifically, if I understood them correctly (given that they are in german) T&C clauses *6.1.7,* 8.4.7, and 8.5 allow Bolt to temporarily suspend driver accounts and restrict access to services where there is a reasonable suspicion of fraud — *this supports the legitimacy of temporarily withholding payouts for manual review (specifically clause 6.1.7.*). Additionally, T&C clause 6.3.6 establishes a clear precedent that suspected fraudulent promo code earnings may be withheld without reimbursement, reinforcing Bolt’s right to adjust or deny payouts linked to fraudulent activity. The availability of a 6-month internal complaint mechanism (clause 8.5) further supports procedural fairness.

However, I think that the rollout of SPR in Switzerland can carry some legal risks. The criteria for flagging fraud must be objectively defined and consistently applied — vague or overly broad triggers could be challenged as unfair or arbitrary. While the drivers are self-employed, Swiss law still imposes duties of good faith and proportionality, especially when it comes to actions that affect remuneration. There is also a risk if legitimate earnings are held back excessively or without sufficient justification, even temporarily.

So just a few questions:

# Do Bolt communicate to affected drivers explaining the hold, its reason, and the resolution timeline? 
# Is only the fraud-flagged portion of earnings is held where possible (rather than full payouts)?

Thanks.

Hello [~accountid:5b8d306bfa38ae2c89608b95], thank you for the provided information. 


This is my POV on this matter:

# *Unilateral changes*

Let's begin with the solution offered by you [~accountid:5b8d306bfa38ae2c89608b95]: Bolt retain the right to unilaterally change the General Terms. Whatever requires negotiation and mutual approval should be reflected in the Special Terms.

*Only if this is a truly no-go for RIMI, then we can offer a solution*: Bolt has the right to update the T&C unilaterally, but Rimi may notify Bolt within x days that it does not agree with the changes, in which case the terms of the previous contract would remain in force.



# *Responsibility for Goods*

Rimi should be explained that even if Rimi and the couriers do not have a direct contract, a courier has an agreement with 1) clients (eaters) who order the food for the delivery services and 2) with Bolt for the platform services. Therefore, when performing their duties, couriers must act not only in accordance with legal acts, but also in accordance with the T&C.

The delivery standard is also set in the T&Cs for Delivery Partners:

* 3.2. The Delivery Partner is solely responsible for complying with all relevant laws and regulations for operating and using the chosen means of transport (e.g. licenses, insurances, etc). Furthermore, the Delivery Partners shall ensure, where relevant, that its authorised persons have all equipment and means that are necessary to perform the delivery services.
* 4.2. The Delivery Partner warrants that during the course of providing the delivery service, the Delivery Partner shall comply and, where relevant, shall ensure that its authorised persons comply, with all relevant laws and regulations applicable to the provision of delivery service to the Client. When authorised persons provide delivery services in the name and on behalf of the Delivery Partner, the Delivery Partner undertakes to (i) fully adhere to any applicable laws and regulations relating to those authorised persons’ health and safety; (ii) ensure that such authorised persons are adequately insured during provision of the delivery services rendered under the Delivery Agreement (including in respect of any means and/or equipment necessary for providing the delivery services); (iii) ensure full compliance with all applicable employment related laws and regulations, where applicable, regarding parental rights, workplace safety, working time, minimum wage or others as well as any tax laws. Furthermore, the Delivery Partner shall attend and, where relevant, shall ensure that its authorised persons shall attend, training(s), pass appropriate exam(s) and maintain all licences, permits, registrations and approvals required for the lawful provision of service(s) pursuant to Delivery Agreements under the applicable law.
* 5.1. The Delivery Partner has to pick up the accepted Order at the time and location indicated on the Bolt Food Platform. The Delivery Partner shall make sure that the right Order is picked up (if necessary, confirming it with the Partner). An accepted Order may be cancelled by the Delivery Partner before the Order has been picked up by the Delivery Partner. In such cases the Delivery Partner is not entitled to the fees under section 7.
* 5.2. In case the Goods contain food, the Delivery Partner has to place the food, which is previously packaged by the Partner, into a thermo-bag without adding or removing any packaging, in order to guarantee that the Goods are delivered in a safe condition, as to ensure health and food safety. The Delivery Partner shall make certain before each delivery of food that the thermo-bag is clean and in good order and is used in a manner that ensures food and health safety and prevents the contamination of food.
* 6.2. In accordance with the Delivery Agreement, the Delivery Partner has to hand over the Order to the Client at the Drop-Off Location. For the purposes of delivering the Order the Delivery Partner can contact the Client throughout the delivery by calling the Client or by using the chat function on the Bolt Food Platform. If the Client fails to take possession of the Order, the Delivery Partner has to contact the Client on the phone number indicated on the Bolt Food Platform on at least 3 separate occasions and stay with the Order at the Drop-Off Location during a 5 minute time frame. If the Client is still unavailable and unable to take possession of the Order, the Delivery Partner will contact Bolt’s customer service in order to authorise Bolt to cancel the Order and fully charge the Client for the Order (including Delivery Fee), as well as to receive further advice regarding the Order.
* etc.



At the same time, it would be good if [~accountid:5fc110f331795a006f947e12] could explain what Bolt is doing to help ensure that couriers are fulfilling their duties properly — for example, how we monitor or support them. Thank you!

Sharing some performance data (like the percentage of successful deliveries) could also help reassure Rimi that things are working well.

To resolve this issue, we can also suggest adding a clause to the agreement that says something like: “Bolt is not responsible for the goods, but will make reasonable efforts to help resolve any issues related to deliveries in a friendly manner.” This would be in line with what’s already stated in the T&C about handling complaints.



# *Customer Issue Resolution and Deductions*

 I see this as more of a technical issue than a legal one. If possible, I would suggest that the business work with Rimi to resolve this issue.
It is also possible that Rimi does not understand the extent of communication with customers and how each confirmation to Rimi will complicate daily operations.
In order to find a solution (if Rimi's requirements are even technically feasible on Bolt’s side), a compromise clause could be included in the agreement (something like that): ‘Bolt shall coordinate solutions with Rimi only for orders exceeding X euros. If Bolt does not receive a response from Rimi within 30 minutes, Bolt shall have the right to act at its own discretion,’ etc.



# *Alcohol Sales and Legal Compliance*

I completely agree that the courier must comply with the law and the requirements set out in the T&C regarding alcohol delivery. However, in this case, I do not believe that Bolt can or should be held responsible for this.

We can explain to Rimi that T&Cs for Delivery Partners include clauses and obligations related to alcohol sales and ID verification. Bolt enforces compliance through contractual commitments with couriers:

* 6.3. In case the Order contains alcohol, tobacco, energy drinks or any other products requiring age verification under the applicable law, it is the Delivery Partner’s obligation to verify that the Client is old enough to legally purchase the products by checking a valid photo identification of the Client before handing over the products (if applicable). In case the Client is not old enough or does not present a valid photo identification, the Delivery Partner may not hand over the products. Furthermore, if the Client is showing signs of intoxication, the Delivery Partner may not hand over the products.
* 6.4. In case the delivery of alcohol is restricted during a particular time slot, it is the Delivery Partner’s responsibility to hand over the alcohol to the Client only during the times allowed under applicable laws.

 

Rimi should once again be informed that the courier is the one responsible in these cases. It’s also important to explain what Bolt is doing to ensure that couriers follow the correct procedures — for example, how we train them to check information properly before handing over goods and etc. [~accountid:5fc110f331795a006f947e12] could you please also explain this part a bit broader? Thank you. 

The goal is to show Rimi that couriers are doing their job responsibly and in line with the required standards.

 

# *Sustainability and Contractual Obligations*

It’s currently unclear which specific clauses Rimi believes are missing from the agreement, so we should ask them to clarify what exactly they feel is missing and what kind of wording they would like to include.

** *Question*: Can Bolt ask the driver for his criminal records?

+*THOUGHTS*+

* Processing criminal offence data, so A10 GDPR applies - need to refer to local law. Per high-level legal research:
** Bolt cannot request the criminal records data from the Information Centre of the Ministry of Interior (the Punishment Register). Bolt can only request it from the driver directly.
** Consent is not an appropriate legal basis for processing the data under Latvian law.
** Even if the driver hands over the records directly, Bolt can only process it if (i) *Latvian national law requires or permits* the processing; and (ii) the *processing is proportionate*, and includes appropriate safeguards. This applies even if the driver provides such records voluntarily.
* As such, not advisable to request criminal records data unless Bolt is explicitly legally permitted to do so. Given that we are not even sure that this driver is the same person, this seems inadvisable on the facts. ❌

Under Portuguese and EU law, nationals from other EU Member States are entitled to work in Portugal without the need for a visa or work permit. However, they must still provide valid documentation proving their identity and residence status.

Relevant documents:

* *Valid EU National ID Card or Passport;*
* *Portuguese Tax Identification Number (NIF) -* required for any individual working or receiving income in Portugal;
* *Portuguese Social Security Number (NISS) -* Required for proper social security contributions;
* *Proof of Address in Portugal* - Confirms place of residence for legal and insurance purposes (acceptable documents: Utility bill, rental contract, or Junta de Freguesia residency certificate); 
* *Registration Certificate for EU Nationals* (Certificado de Registo de Cidadão da UE) - Required for stays in Portugal longer than 90 days (standard for employment).



Important Note:

If the courier is operating under a service provision contract (prestação de serviços), where he is providing services to the fleet operator, proof of activity with AT (i.e., registration as independent worker) may also be required.

Thank you!

Please see my questions to the externals and their answers regarding the drafts:

# Why the part of first instance reporting through standard Bolt reporting procedures has been removed (clause 2.4.1. of the Global policy draft)?

According to the local law implementing the WB Directive, the internal reporting channel must by design protect the confidentiality of the identity of the whistleblower and of any third party mentioned in the report, and to prevent access to the report by unauthorized personnel. This standard of protection is not met by contacting via slack, phone, service desk, in person, or email your superior or the HR department. The risk to Bolt is that the employee reasonably considers that the internal reporting setup in not safe from the possibility of retaliation or being exposed, in which case he/she is entitled to go directly to the authorities or to take matters public, without Bolt being able to hold him/her liable for breaching any confidentiality or similar obligation. Our advice is to be very clear that only the designated person is entitled to receive reports.

# Who should be designated person and who and how to designate him? Is it enough to mention it only in the policy? 

There is no legal determination, any person best placed to handle and coordinate reports can be designated, a special department, even third parties. There should be a formal designation by Ahto, as director of the company. We usually draft a director's decision whereby both the policy and the designated person are approved.

# Can we designate several designated persons? Can they be from other Bolt entities, for example, our HQ entity in Estonia?

Yes, there is no limitation, but please note that the designated person has the right to discuss directly with the designated person and the designated person has the obligation to keep evidence of the reports and escalate to the authorities in case criminal wrongdoing must be reported. It may be easier for someone local to be at least part of the department, but if it is not possible, please let us liaise with the designated person from HQ and we will assist them.

# In RO policy draft it is stated that Ethics committee will receive report and designate investigator (2.4.1. and 2.5.2.) which is also in line with the Global policy draft although in Investigation Handbook it is mentioned that Designated Person will receive all reports as sole administrator of this tool (Section 2). Can we have similar process in Romania that Global Ethics committee is receiving these reports but they will assign specific Designated Person for the Romanian cases? I will check but I am not sure if we will be able to configure our whistleblower tool to send Romanian cases straight to Designated person avoiding Ethics Committee.

We can draft such a mechanism, but in this case the entire Ethics committee will act as the designated department. The Designated Person cannot share the reports with other persons who do not formally have this role and corresponding obligations. Let me know if this works.

# The payout balance and status is displayed on the driver app with relevant state visibility. They will also see once the payout has been processed and ‘handed over' to their bank to be processed. 

Additionally, driver will see the refunds/deductions totals (= all adjustments, not just fraud) on their driver app balance section. We avoid pointing to exactly which journeys are actioned by us due to it being direct clue to those wishing to take advantage of our systems and trying to find which and how we detect. 

It is also available for agents who communicate with partners to inform of the decisions timeline, especially when to expect a final conclusion. Majority of cases, we have already conducted reviews even before the partner notices. 

E.g. [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/360012567634?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/360012567634?country=global&language=en] covers any questions and processes CS can perform regarding payouts altogether. 

In order to limit informing career fraudsters on what and how we detect, any information around fraud actions is limited and basic - we often refer to non adherence to the T&C. However, there are guidelines that upon need the partner can raise a case regarding their earnings and in turn CS can provide the relevant answers to their questions as well as consult further with our team via service desk upon suspecting the need for further review or gaining further context/evidence to driver behaviour. 


2. Technically we cannot separate any irregular nor good earnings into a separate bucket. What currently happens is that a payout gets composed based on the partner running balance at the designated time (e.g. 23:59 Sunday) which amounts are then taken from the balance and composed onto a ‘payout’. While going through numerous other payout related flows (where there can be rejections or delays as well - due to operations, technical etc reasons), the payout also flows through our fraud checkpoint which, then, based on the carefully analysed patterns, puts the payout on a hold (if no alert, the payout flows on into banks' communications step where our banking solution is triggered to pay onto the details they have made available). When team has found sufficient evidence to say that the payout consists of illegally or maliciously obtained amounts, the payout gets rejected. Upon this rejection, the payout amount gets added back onto driver balance. This means that these amounts that we detected bad are back on the driver’s balance including the other entirety of the previously composed payout. Now, this is the moment the fraud team does refunds and adjustments (deductions) for fraud amounts to level the current balance and remove amounts that are not justified or not earned fairly. Important to note here that majority of scenarios these are amounts that have been left unpaid through manipulation of payments through the collaboration of the rider and driver - cases where Bolt has never recieved any funds for the journeys or received further card disputes (that also have extra license and payment costs to Bolt) for the journeys. So, when we say ‘refund’ it is often just a movement of payment claim and adjustment of driver balance for non-paid amounts. 

It is possible that the driver also has ‘good’ leftover earnings and these remain onto their balance to be treated as the partner sees fit. If the driver requests - they can reach out to CS in order to expedite (recompose) that week’s rest of the amounts again. If not, then automatically the same cycle continues next week and the driver’s past good balance is included in the new payout already as it was on their balance at the time of the composal. So in any case, the driver will receive what they are owed for non-malicious trips (rightful earnings). And as mentioned before, if driver has sufficient reasoning and evidence to support their counterclaims on balance adjustments, these are handled and escalated according to CS processes for further review. 

For extra context, we target the worst of the worst cases where we can see that majority of partners payout ‘may’ consist of fraudulent earnings. These make around 0.4% of the all payouts that qualify to our checks (run through the checks but are never alerted or stopped). For Switzerland, this is estimated to be around 0-3 drivers a week that will need a further manual human check. The hard time-limit of our reviews is 36h at which point if we haven’t made the decision the system automatically proceeds to send out the payouts. Our current average of reviewing is around 5h for European region cases which may be a slight delay felt by the partner - most will not even feel the checks as the banking processing side of payouts often takes 10 times as long and varies per the bank significantly. If we decide there is not sufficient evidence to support driver involvement (we cannot directly or sufficiently connect the driver to the scheme) then we do not touch the money and pay out the amounts. Our stance will remain that only if we can see direct correlations with sufficient impact, we take actions. We look at evidence like driver behaviour before, after and during the order. Their connections to the suspected rider or evidence supporting them taking an advantage of a rider (e.g. _map data suggests never picking them up or we can see that the rider and driver have the same phone number on their account_). Hence, we can conclude that decisions that affect the earnings are only done when there is sufficient reason to do so.

* Upgrade python > 3.9.6

{noformat}pip3 install confluent-kafka==2.5.3{noformat}
* Add this line on .zshrc for root user 
{noformat}if command -v pyenv 1>/dev/null 2>&1; then
  eval "$(pyenv init -)"
fi

export TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR="$HOME/.terraform.d/plugin-cache"

export C_INCLUDE_PATH=/opt/homebrew/include
export LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/homebrew/lib{noformat}

Once all done, this should work:

{noformat}aws sso login --profile db{noformat}

After that, this should also work:

{noformat}aws --profile=db-test ec2 describe-instances | head{noformat}

Hi,
I am basing myself on the relevant taxi regulations of the Regions.


*Brussels:* The main article that list the obligations of a reservation intermediary is article 30 of the ordinance, which says:
_§ 1er. Chaque intermédiaire de réservation doit :_
_1° ne permettre l’enregistrement, pour la prestation de service de taxi,_
_que :_
_a) des exploitants qui disposent de l’autorisation d’exploiter visée_
_à l’article 5 ;_
_b) des chauffeurs qui disposent du certificat de capacité visé à_
_l’article 13 ;_

It does not contain any obligations for the reservation intermediary to check themselves the underlying documents that are required to obtain the “autorisation d’exploiter un service de taxi”. 
Full docs of the ordinance and implementing regulations here: [https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1G4iTLaGmxzS-BE9-fyzBxjD0n6yxRydv|https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1G4iTLaGmxzS-BE9-fyzBxjD0n6yxRydv|smart-link] 



For *Flanders*: regulation [https://www.vlaanderen.be/taxi/taxi-soorten-en-voorwaarden#regelgeving|https://www.vlaanderen.be/taxi/taxi-soorten-en-voorwaarden#regelgeving|smart-link] . It doesn’t contain any specific obligations in this regard on reservation intermediaries. 

For *Wallonia* - to my knowledge also no such obligation on reservation intermediaries, but I haven’t looked at it in detail (can do sop of needed). Ideally, we could dynamically get the list of permissions for each API used in a pipeline and use that to filter which pipelines are displayed for the current user. This would allow us to only display the relevant ones.

Because doing this is non-trivial (requires changes in NJSC Parser and Open API client generator) I suggest a simple solution: introduce in-code a data structure for the “limited roles” which holds roles as keys and arrays of the available pipelines as values. If the user has one or more of the “limited” roles, then we’ll only display the pipelines for those roles. The downside is that if somebody has a limited role and a non-limited role, then they’ll also see a limited number of pipelines. For this, we’ll display a message telling the users when they see only a limited number of pipelines.

This filtering has to be done in the backend.

We conducted an investigation and found the following: The root cause is the use of WebView, and unfortunately, this issue cannot be fixed. Here’s a longer explanation:

On iOS, we encounter a problem due to overlapping scroll areas. If a user touches the message bubbles and tries to scroll, the interaction works as intended—the input text remains attached to the keyboard, and the bubbles scroll as expected. However, the problem most often arises when users perform a scrolling gesture near the input text field. In this case, WebView registers the gesture and attempts to scroll the entire content, including the input text area itself. This results in the input field moving together with the content, which is not the expected behavior. And system does not provide any callbacks to us to intercept the behaviour. This issue doesn’t occur on Android.

Unfortunately, this scrolling behavior is a common limitation when working with scrollable areas inside a WebView on iOS.

*1. “10K Event” – Surprise €5,000 Prize to the 10,000th Branded Car*

Based on Matteo clarification:

* The campaign is *no longer a true "surprise reward"*, but *a publicised prize* awarded based on a *randomized milestone condition*.
* *Eligibility is open* to all drivers receiving stickers during a time-bound campaign.
* The *€5,000 is positioned as a prize*, and not simply a discretionary gift.

This now meets the definition of a *jeu-concours* under French consumer law, correct?

So, per _Code de la consommation_ Articles L121-36 et seq.:

* ✅ A *règlement de jeu is mandatory* (must define the rules, conditions, and prize allocation process).
* ⚠️ A *randomized winner selection with a prize* creates *legal obligations for transparency, fairness, and documentation*.
* 📌 Involving LMDCVTC as the "selector" *does not eliminate* the need for rules and *may not suffice* to ensure legal defensibility in case of a dispute.

If wz do *not publish a règlement*, *we risk a challenge by the DGCCRF* (France’s consumer enforcement body) for misleading or unfair commercial practices.

h3. ✅ *Recommendations*

* *IMMEDIATELY draft and publish* a short *règlement du jeu*, covering:
** Eligibility (e.g., sticker installation between X and Y dates)
** Selection mechanism (objective time-stamped milestone)
** Payment mechanism (including fleet intermediaries)
** Prize value and tax disclaimers
* *Have LMDCVTC issue a dated attestation* confirming the 10,000th sticker application.
* *Consider bailiff deposit of the rules* (“dépôt chez huissier”) to preempt contestability—(this is completely optional) but it strengthens compliance posture.

➡️ *Status: LEGALLY FEASIBLE WITH URGENT REMEDIATION*

* Publicly disclosed prize pool.
* Automatic enrollment based on stickering.
* Random drawing of winners.
* Defined prize and date window (end of July).

----

* A *règlement de jeu is mandatory*, per French law.
* It *must be published and made accessible* to participants.
* A *drawing process must be documented* and ideally validated by a third party (bailiff optional but recommended).
* T&Cs must include:
** The number and value of prizes
** Selection date and method
** Payout mechanics
** Dispute resolution info
** Exclusion of fraud or duplicate entries

Hi [~accountid:712020:e7c4988a-ccaf-44c1-8546-2d01d1217937], many thanks again for confirming that you are happy with proceeding on an exclusive basis as well as the other points above.

+*Key Legal Risks to Flag*+

# *Fee is payable even if Devono didn’t introduce the property* (*clause 3.4*): As flagged previously, the current wording provides that Devono still receives its full fee during the exclusivity period even if we find the property ourselves or through another source. 
→ We recommend pushing back on this in the first instance so that they only get paid if they’ve materially helped with the introduction, inspection, or negotiation of the property, and we have provisionally amended this clause in the marked-up copy.
# *Devono can charge fees even after we terminate them* (*clause 6.2*): If we terminate the agreement, Devono can still claim a fee for any properties they introduced - *even months later*.
→ We understand from your response above that you are comfortable with paying a non-exclusive fee if we terminate (provided it is no more than the original agreed fee), however this fee should not be due if we we terminate due to performance issues. We have incorporated your comments into the marked-up draft. 
→ We also recommend limiting Devono being able to claim a fee to: 3 months after the termination (as opposed to indefinitely), and we have reflected this in the marked-up copy.
# *High abortive fees if a deal falls through* (*clause 5.2*): If we pull out of a deal after agreeing heads of terms (but before contracts), we could be charged *50–100% of the full fee*. 
→ Has this abortive fee already been discussed with Devono? 
→ Are you comfortable with this abortive fee? If not, subject to your thoughts and whether or not Devono would be willing to accept a lower cap, *we can look to cap the abortive fee at a lower sum (e.g. £10k-£20k), or remove the abortive fee altogether. Please confirm and we will amend the terms in redline accordingly.* 
# *Fees are calculated on headline rent - not what we actually pay* (*clauses 5.3 and 5.4*): The current clauses ignore any rent-free periods, landlord contributions, or other incentives we negotiate.
→ We recommend revising these clauses to ensure that fees are based on *net effective rent*, i.e what Bolt is actually paying, not inflated figures. We have provisionally amended these clauses in the marked-up copy.
# *Liability cap* (*clause 7.3*): Devono’s liability is capped at the amount of their fee (i.e. the most we can recover from Devono is the total fee we pay them, even if their breach/error costs us significantly more). 
→ We recommend +increasing+ Devono’s liability cap (so that we have the ability to claim as much as possible in the event of breach etc). +We have amended the marked-up copy to include a liability cap of £500k.+ Please ensure that this is acceptable from your perspective. 

+*Commercial/Operational Points for Your Review*+

# *Scope of Services* *(pg 1 - 2 of the Engagement Letter):* please review the list of services that Devono will provide and confirm that you are aligned with the scope of services listed in the letter.
# *Fee:* the fee options (set out on page 2 of the Engagement Letter) are either “+Option 1+:  Fee of 5.25% of the agreed headline rent. The fee will be capped at £120,000.” or  “+Option 2+:  Fixed fee of £115,000.” Please confirm which fee option you would like to opt for and ensure that you select one of the options when signing the Engagement Letter. 
# *Additional space charges* (*clause 5.5*): if we acquire more space in the same building within 12 months, Devono may charge an additional fee.
→ Are we planning potential expansion in the building? If yes, we may want to *carve this out* and we have provisionally amended clause 5.5 to state that “this clause shall apply only where the additional space is acquired as a result of Devono’s direct involvement, introduction, or negotiation.” *Please confirm whether this amendment is relevant.* 
# *Invoices must be paid within 30 days of issuing (clause 5.7):* we assume that this is acceptable in practice and we are just flagging for your information. Please let us know if this is not the case.
# *Devono disclaims all responsibility for property suitability and information accuracy* (*clauses 8.1 - 8.3*): please note that Devono puts full responsibility for checking title, planning, square footage, etc. on Bolt.

+*Next Steps*+

Please let me know if you have any questions (either on the things you have flagged or the amendments suggested). Please also confirm whether we should make any amendments to clause 5.2 (as flagged above). 

If you do not have any questions or comments, please send the marked-up copy to Debono for their approval (copy attached to this ticket).  

Best wishes

Catherine

Hi, there was an issue where the drivers did not receive their payouts so they made and early cashout. Because of that, they have a negative balance now, and covered it, but they still saw a negative balance and the negative balance was covered by finishing the trips.

+*THOUGHTS*+

*Review of DPA correspondence* (/) 

* Correspondence with the DPA suggests “_The use of dash cams by anyone is currently prohibited as there is no legal framework/legal basis… inside …would disproportionately interfere with the privacy of citizens (taxi drivers and passengers)_.”
* According to quick research ([here|https://www.lawyersincyprus.com/gdpr-and-cctv-monitoring-in-cyprus-ensuring-gdpr-compliance/#:~:text=Currently%20there%20is%20no%20specific,consent%20of%20the%20affected%20individuals.] and [here|https://economoulegal.com/publications/gdpr-and-video-surveillance-in-cyprus-ensuring-privacy-compliance]):
** There is indeed no current specific legislative framework governing the use of dash cams.
** Dashcams can only be used in Cyprus with DS *consent*: “_there is no specific legislative framework governing the use of cameras in Cyprus. According to the Commissioner’s guidelines, the legal basis for processing… images and/or audio from dash cams is the prior consent of the affected individuals. Without such consent, such processing violates GDPR principles of legality, purpose limitation, and data minimization_”
** *Transparency* is key: “_warning signs should be prominently displayed to inform persons that such recordings are taking place_”
** Other usual principles apply (e.g., right to access, proportionality, retention etc.).
* Even though the email chain refers to dashcams as ‘prohibited’, it also refers to the DPA’s guidance from 2019 - such guidance mirrors the research findings above (i.e., there +_is_+ a legal basis - consent). As such, the correspondence is a bit misleading.
* In any case, these obligations apply to the controller. If Bolt has positioned itself in the usual way (i.e., the driver is the controller) then Bolt does not need to worry about this.
* *Conclusion*: Bolt itself does not need to worry about legal basis / transparency etc. Driver must ensure consent / transparency.

*Review of Bolt templates* (/) 

* Rider template:
** Broad position is correct insofar as drivers are the data controller. Could do with some minor tweaking to emphasise controller position.
** Worth including an additional note saying that we have reached out to the driver to remind them of their obligations. This is the approach we have taken in the past, and helps to de-escalate things. It also reflects what we are actually doing here (as we are reaching out to the driver anyway).
** Not sure it is worth giving the user the contact details of lots of different authorities (unless mandatory) - this will only escalate matters further. Instead, we should just flag that the user can complain to the relevant authorities, and we would be willing to cooperate.
* Driver template:
** The response treads the correct legal line in terms of maintaining controllership position. However, some minor tweaks could reinforce this.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

*Revised Rider Template:*

Please note that drivers are not Bolt employees and Bolt does not control what drivers are able to record on a CCTV camera that they own. This underlines their responsibility to ensure that their use of a CCTV camera aligns with relevant requirements.
In the interests of addressing your concerns, we have passed them on to the driver. We are also fully prepared to cooperate with any investigation, should you wish to contact the relevant authorities in relation to this matter (we can be contacted directly by any relevant authorities at [cyauthority@bolt.eu|mailto:cyauthority@bolt.eu]).

Please be aware that non-compliance with these requirements could potentially lead to legal consequences due to breaches of privacy laws.

The [document|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1lQLId9tyJXjHswPUIP2YTcrMn7b0i6X4VuS9lfwe_iQ/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.47s0olh63qps] describes possible on-board self-test procedures that IOT could carry out to give feedback of any possible faulty components on the scooter.

*NB! There is no spec for this function yet* 🙂 *, it is on best effort basis. It would be good to have a simple POC running fast and then the usability of the whole idea can be tested. If it proves useful then more test steps can be added.*

How the function works:

* The whole point of having the self-test state handling and result analysis on IOT is to give fast and responsive feedback to rider. Sound and IOT display elements can be used to show the selft-test mode state - for example, which test step is running, what is expected from user.
* IOT defines BE-IOT protocol new command(s) and status elements to
** Start the self-test mode (and/or test steps within the test mode). Any following PowerOn or PowerOff command with cancel the test mode. The test mode must have a clear indication on the screen that test mode is active, for example blinking exclamation mark.
* Since IOT UI is very limited,  the app UI must be the one that leads the test-person through the process. The app must test what the user should do and the IOT.



My suggestion is to start be making a throttle-brake test:

# A command (maybe PowerOn with a special parameter) puts scooter into test mode
## Command fails if wheelspeed is not 0
## If wheelspeed 0, IOT puts exclamation mark blinking and Shows S1 on display (if wheelspeed changes to above 0, then it shows speed)
## While standing still:
### IOT audio instructs to press throttle to full. If not reached within timeout, step failed
### IOT audio instructs to press left brake to full. If not reached within timeout, step failed
### IOT audio instructs to press right brake to full. If not reached within timeout, step failed
## Ride:
### IOT audio instructs to accelerate to 15km/h and then brake to full stop without skidding (15km/h reached could be indicated by beeping?). IOT measures wheelspeed drop from 15 to 0. Gets a ballpark estimate if brakes work

Abu Dhabi:

Under the UAE PDPL (Federal Law No. 45/2021):

* Cross-border transfers are *allowed without notification or authorisation* _only_ if the receiving country is *deemed adequate* by the UAE Data Office.
* If the destination is *not adequate*, transfers must rely on *approved safeguards* (e.g. SCCs or BCRs).
* If no adequacy or safeguards exist, the organisation must *obtain prior authorisation* from the UAE Data Office before transferring data.

Because the *adequacy list is not yet published*, most transfers currently require *either safeguards or permission*, so *authorisation is effectively required*.

Azerbaijan:

Under Azerbaijan’s *Law No. 998‑IIIQ on Personal Data (May 2010)*:

* Cross-border transfers are *prohibited* unless:
** The *destination country* legally ensures a level of personal data protection comparable to Azerbaijan’s, *or*
** The transfer is based on explicit *safeguards*, such as contractual terms or data subject consent 
* There is *no requirement* for prior *notification or authorisation* from the DPA — the law instead relies on these conditions for legality .

Because there’s *no registration, notification, or permit regime* tied to cross-border moves — only conditional legal grounds — the answer for authorisation is *No*.

*Ontario (PIPEDA)*:

* Cross-border data transfers are treated as a *"use"*, not a "disclosure" — *no separate consent or authorisation* required.
* Organisations remain *accountable* and must use *contracts or other means* to ensure a "comparable level of protection" while data is processed by third parties, whether domestic or international.

*No notification to* or *approval from* the Office of the Privacy Commissioner (OPC) is required.


*Québec (Law 25)*:

* Requires a *Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA)* for cross-border transfers.
** Must enter into a *contract* with the foreign service provider ensuring adequate protection.
** No formal *notification or authorisation* from Québec’s data protection authority (CAI) is needed — obligations are internal and contractual.

Egypt:


Egypt’s *PDPL (Law No. 151/2020)* mandates that personal data *cannot be transferred* outside the country *unless*:

* The destination country ensures a *comparable level of protection* to Egypt’s, *or*
* A *licence or permit* is obtained from the *Personal Data Protection Center*, *or*
* A specific *exception applies* (e.g., data subject consent, contractual necessity, public interest) 
* The law explicitly *requires prior authorisation* (licence/permit) or proof of adequacy — *no mere notification option exists* .

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. The reversal can take up to 14 days depending on the bank internal processes. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount.

To summarise our last meeting:

*The offer*:

* Offer within the Bronze Tiers to make it accessible to all drivers;
* Offer water bottles that would be Bolt branded and/or unbranded and/or branded with the partner’s distributor name;
* Bolt would participate in the offer and provide a financial compensation to the partner in order to make the offer attractive to drivers (example of what we did with Electra).

 

*Question to review*:

* If we offer Bolt-branded water bottle packs, does this increase the risk of reclassification?
* If Bolt financially contributes to this initiative, does this increase the risk of reclassification?
* Can we offer a subscription based offer: ie. 3-months subscription instead of a monthly subscription?

 

*Mitigating measures*:

* I would make this a *“Limited offer”*;
* Between the branded and unbranded offers, *nothing is presented as a “recommended” option by Bolt*.
* In order to restrict the accumulation of programs and branded products, at least in the initial test phase I would exclude drivers part of the Brand Program from this offer: *“Bolt branded cars are not eligible to this offer”*;
* Include a disclaimer of optionality on any communication: *_“Participation in this offer is entirely optional and does not constitute a requirement or expectation under the Bolt driver-partner agreement”_*_;_ 
* Include a disclaimer that Bolt is not the seller: *“**_This offer is facilitated via the Bolt Rewards platform as a third-party benefit, provided by [Partner Name]. Bolt does not guarantee availability, pricing, or fulfillment.”_*

 

I think that we could offer such an offer to drivers, provided that:

* the drivers have the choice between branded and unbranded bottles → or co-branded if possible;
* the mitigating measures are implemented;
* to reduce Bolt’s financial contribution, our financial participation should not be indefinite.

If the user doesn’t answer both questions correctly, we ask them 2 more questions:

* What is the phone number registered to your account?
* What was the price of your last order?

* What is the email address registered to your account?

New Zealand:

[Principle 12|http://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2020/0031/latest/LMS23376.html] sets rules around sending personal information to organisations or people outside New Zealand.

Principle 12 is a new principle in the Privacy Act 2020.

A business or organisation may only disclose personal information to another organisation outside New Zealand if they check that the receiving organisation:

* is subject to the Privacy Act because they do business in New Zealand
* will adequately protect the information, e.g. by using [model contract clauses|https://www.privacy.org.nz/responsibilities/your-obligations/disclosing-personal-information-outside-new-zealand/], or
* is subject to privacy laws that provide comparable safeguards to the Privacy Act

If none of the above criteria apply, a business or organisation may only make a cross-border disclosure with the permission of the person concerned. The person must be expressly informed that their information may not be given the same protection as provided by the New Zealand Privacy Act.

The goal is to make sure that the privacy protections that individuals can reasonably expect under New Zealand’s Privacy Act continue to apply when their information is disclosed and used in a different country.

Nigeria:


* *Section 41(1)*: Transfers are only allowed if the recipient has:
** Adequate protection via law, BCRs, contractual clauses, codes, or certifications; *or*
** A fallback legal basis like *explicit consent*, contract performance, legal claims, or vital/public interest.
* *Section 41(2)*: The controller/processor must *document* the basis and adequacy.
* *Section 41(3)*: The *NDPC* *_may_* require *notification* of these measures — but this is not automatic or pre-transfer.
* *Section 42–43*: The *NDPC can determine* adequacy or approve safeguards — but absence of such a determination does *not block transfers*, if other legal bases apply.
* There is *no requirement to seek DPA (NDPC) authorisation* before making transfers.

Paraguay:

The Personal Credit Data Protection Law establishes that international transfers of personal data to a recipient that is in a third country (as defined under the Law),  or to an international organization where the guarantees, requirements and/or exceptions established in the Law are not met, is a violation of applicable data protection law and, thus, can be subject to sanctions (Art. 21.x. of the Law).

Under current legislation, there are no other specific provisions that regulate the transfer of private information. However, the transfer of private information is considered as a form of data processing, so the same rules than for collection and processing personal data applies (Art. 3.e. of the Law – definition treatment of data).

Saudi Arabia:

There are detailed rules relating to the transfer of personal data outside of KSA. The PDPL allows for the transfer of personal data outside of KSA for several purposes (for example, if such action is taken to meet an obligation to which the data subject is a party) and subject to various conditions (for example, the transfer or disclosure must not compromise the national security or vital interests of KSA and be limited to the minimum amount of personal data needed).

Subject to such requirements and conditions, the Transfer Regulations have introduced a number of circumstances where a cross border transfer of personal data is permissible. This includes to countries with appropriate levels of protection and no less than the protections afforded under the PDPL.

However, transfers of personal data to countries which are not deemed as having an adequate level of protection may still be made where "appropriate safeguards" are put in place. If the data controller is unable to use any of the appropriate safeguards, there are still limited cases where cross border transfers are permissible. Such transfers are still however subject to various controls.

In certain contexts or sectors, specific approvals may be required – for example, in a banking context, approval from the Saudi Central Bank. Data held by telecommunications, postal and IT service providers or government agencies may also be subject to additional restrictions.

Thailand

Under *Thailand’s PDPA*, cross-border transfers are permitted if:

* The destination offers *equivalent protection* under law; *or*
* Appropriate *safeguards* (e.g., *Binding Corporate Rules*, *Standard Contractual Clauses*) are implemented; *or*
* A legal exception applies (e.g., *data subject consent*, contract performance, public interest).
* *Ride-hailing data* (e.g. passenger location, trip logs, driver IDs) qualifies as *personal* or *sensitive personal data* under PDPA and must be:
** Collected and transferred based on a *lawful basis*,
** Accompanied by a *risk assessment*,
** Properly documented in Records of Processing Activities (ROPA),
** Shared only under *contractual guarantees*.
* There is *no requirement to notify or obtain authorisation* from the *PDPC* per transfer — instead, controllers must *self-assess and document* compliance.

[https://www.legal500.com/developments/thought-leadership/thailands-personal-data-protection-overview-and-updates/|https://www.legal500.com/developments/thought-leadership/thailands-personal-data-protection-overview-and-updates/]
